description_full: The Southern Company, through its subsidiaries, engages in the sale of electricity. The company offers electric service to retail customers and wholesale customers; and energy-related products and services to natural gas choice markets. It also develops, constructs, acquires, owns, operates, and manages power generation assets, as well as battery energy storage projects; sells electricity at market-based rates in the wholesale market; and deploys microgrids for commercial, industrial, governmental, and utility customers. In addition, the company is involved in the distribution of natural gas in Illinois, Georgia, Virginia, and Tennessee; distributes energy and resilience solutions; and invests in telecommunications. The Southern Company was incorporated in 1945 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

financial_summary: Southern Company (The) is a large-cap utilities business with a $109.0B market cap on $29.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.
The company is burning through $2.9B of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.3%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.0) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent

Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk
